# **Item-by-item evaluation**

For each item, we assess how closely the proposed method reproduces the **relative ranking of normalization methods** established by the gold standard.

Because the gold standard may contain **ties (methods assigned the same rank)**, we use metrics that can accommodate tied rankings.

## Kendall's rank correlation (tau)

### Definition

Kendall's rank correlation measures agreement between two rankings by comparing the relative order of all pairs of items.

It accounts for:

* Concordant pairs (same order)
* Discordant pairs (reversed order)
* Ties through an adjustment

### What it assesses

* **Overall agreement between rankings**
* Consistency across pairwise comparisons
* Agreement when the gold standard contains ties

### Interpretation

| Value   | Interpretation      |
| ------- | ------------------- |
| > 0.7   | Very high agreement |
| 0.6–0.7 | High agreement      |
| 0.4–0.6 | Moderate agreement  |
| < 0.4   | Low agreement       |

This is the most **stringent and conservative** metric.

## Spearman's rank correlation (rho)

### Definition

Spearman's rank correlation measures the association between two sets of values by converting them to ranks and calculating the correlation between those ranks.

### What it assesses

* The **overall structure of the rankings**
* The general ordering trend
* Agreement with less sensitivity to small differences in rank than Kendall's correlation

### Interpretation

| Value   | Interpretation      |
| ------- | ------------------- |
| > 0.8   | Very high agreement |
| 0.7–0.8 | High agreement      |
| 0.5–0.7 | Moderate agreement  |

This metric is intermediate in stringency.

## Pairwise accuracy

### Definition

Pairwise accuracy considers all pairs of normalization methods for which the gold standard establishes a clear order, excluding ties. It is the proportion of those pairs for which the proposed method reproduces the same order.

### What it assesses

* How often the proposed method reproduces the **clear preferences established by the gold standard**
* Agreement among pairs with a clear reference order
* Relative ordering between individual methods

### Interpretation

| Value     | Interpretation |
| --------- | -------------- |
| > 0.85    | Excellent      |
| 0.75–0.85 | High           |
| 0.65–0.75 | Good           |
| ≈ 0.5     | Near chance    |

This is the most **robust and interpretable** metric in the presence of ties.

# **Overall evaluation**

At this level, we assess how well normScore identifies the **best and worst normalization methods** without requiring it to reproduce the full ranking.

The gold standard defines two sets of methods:

* Recommended normalization methods (best)
* Normalization methods to avoid (worst)

## Hit@k (Top)

### Definition

For each dataset, Hit@k indicates whether at least one normalization method recommended by the gold standard appears among the top *k* positions in the normScore ranking. It is 1 if at least one recommended method appears in the top *k* and 0 otherwise. Averaged across datasets, Hit@k is the proportion of datasets for which this occurs.

### What it assesses

* The ability to **identify at least one recommended method**
* Performance in practical settings where identifying one good option is sufficient

### Interpretation

* Values close to 1 indicate that at least one recommended method is found in the top *k* for most datasets.
* Performance is interpreted relative to the expected value under random ranking.

For example, with eight methods and **one** method recommended by the gold standard:

* The chance of a Top-1 hit is 12.5%.
* Values substantially above this baseline indicate better-than-chance performance.

## Bottom Coverage (Worst)

### Definition

Bottom coverage measures how many of the normalization methods flagged for exclusion by the gold standard appear among the lowest-ranked methods in the normScore ranking.

It can be expressed as:

* The number of methods correctly placed among the lowest-ranked positions
* The proportion of all methods flagged for exclusion that appear in those positions

### What it assesses

* The ability to identify **methods that should be avoided**
* Agreement at the bottom of the ranking

---

### Interpretation

| Proportion      | Interpretation         |
| --------------- | ---------------------- |
| 1.0             | Complete coverage      |
| 0.75 to < 1.0   | High coverage          |
| 0.50 to < 0.75  | Moderate coverage      |
| < 0.50          | Low coverage           |

This metric is particularly relevant when deciding which normalization methods to exclude.

## Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)

### Definition

For each dataset, the reciprocal rank is the inverse of the position of the first normalization method recommended by the gold standard. For example, the reciprocal rank is:

* 1 if the first recommended method is ranked first
* 1/2 if it is ranked second
* 1/3 if it is ranked third

The mean reciprocal rank (MRR) is the average of these values across datasets.

### What it assesses

* How high the first recommended method appears in the ranking
* How far down the ranking one must look to find a recommended method

### Interpretation

* Values close to 1 indicate that a recommended method usually appears near the top of the ranking.
* With eight methods and **one** recommended method, the expected MRR under random ranking is approximately 0.34.

| MRR            | Interpretation |
| -------------- | -------------- |
| > 0.60         | Very high      |
| 0.50–0.60      | High           |
| 0.40 to < 0.50 | Moderate       |
| Near chance    | Low            |

## Results

Results for unweighted normScore across all 100 datasets in the gold-standard collection are presented separately for the identification of recommended methods (top) and methods to avoid (bottom).

### Jacqquar index {.tabset}

```{r}

# R1 vs normScore
jacIndR1NS <- sapply(names(resAllGS$globalBests), function(i) 
  jaccardTopSet(
    rankedMethods = resAllNS$resGlobal[[i]], 
    referenceSet = resAllGS$globalBests[[i]]
  )
)

# R2 vs normScore
jacIndR2NS <- sapply(names(resAllGSR2$globalBests), function(i) 
  jaccardTopSet(
    rankedMethods = resAllNS$resGlobal[[i]], 
    referenceSet = resAllGSR2$globalBests[[i]]
  )
)

# R1 vs R2
jacIndR1R2 <- sapply(names(resAllGSR2$globalBests), function(i) 
  jaccardIndex(
    setA = resAllGS$globalBests[[i]], 
    setB = resAllGSR2$globalBests[[i]]
  )
)


dfJI <- data.frame(
  Datasets = names(jacIndR1NS), 
  R1NS = jacIndR1NS[names(jacIndR1NS)],
  R2NS = jacIndR2NS[names(jacIndR1NS)],
  R1R2 = jacIndR1R2[names(jacIndR1NS)]
)


dfJaccard <- dfJI %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = -Datasets,
    names_to = "Comparison", 
    values_to = "Jaccard index"
  )

dfJaccard$Comparison <- factor(
      dfJaccard$Comparison,
      levels = c(
        "R1NS", 
        "R2NS", 
        "R1R2"
      ),
      labels = c(
        "NormScore vs Review 1",
        "NormScore vs Review 2",
        "Review 1 vs Review 2"
      )
    )

dfJaccardCount <- dfJaccard %>%
  count(Comparison, `Jaccard index`) %>%
  mutate(`Jaccard index` = round(`Jaccard index`, 2)) %>%
  tidyr::complete(
    Comparison,
    `Jaccard index`,
    # `Jaccard index` = jaccardLevels,
    fill = list(n = 0)
  )


df <- dfJaccard %>% 
  group_by(Comparison)  %>%
  summarise(
    Median = median(`Jaccard index`), 
    IQR = IQR(`Jaccard index`), 
    Mean = mean(`Jaccard index`), 
    SD = sd(`Jaccard index`), 
    Minimum = min(`Jaccard index`),
    Maximum = max(`Jaccard index`)
  )



DT::datatable(df, extensions = "Buttons", rownames = F, escape = F,
            options = list(ordering = T, dom = "Brt", scrollY = F,
                            scrollX = F, pageLength = nrow(df),
                            columnDefs = list(list(className = 'dt-center', targets = '_all')),
                            full_width = TRUE, rowCallback = DT::JS(js),
                            buttons = list(list(extend = "copy", text = "Copiar"),
                            list(extend = "csv"),
                            list(extend = "excel")),
                            language = list(url = "https://cdn.datatables.net/plug-ins/1.11.5/i18n/es-ES.json"))) |> 
DT::formatStyle(1, font = 'bold') %>%
  DT::formatRound(2:6, 2)
df <- dfJaccard  
colnames(df)[3] <- "JI"
res <- Biostatech::tableDescr(formula = Comparison ~ JI, data = df, id.var = "Datasets")
Biostatech::postHocAnalysis(tabla = res$tabla, df = df, varGroup = Comparison)
```

#### Boxplot {-}

```{r include=FALSE}
comparisonsList <- list(
  c("Review 1 vs Review 2", "NormScore vs Review 1"),
  c("Review 1 vs Review 2", "NormScore vs Review 2"),
  c("NormScore vs Review 1", "NormScore vs Review 2")
)


id_col <- "Datasets"
stopifnot(id_col %in% names(dfJaccard))

testsJaccard <- do.call(rbind, lapply(comparisonsList, function(grupos) {
  g1 <- dfJaccard[dfJaccard$Comparison %in% grupos[1], ]
  g2 <- dfJaccard[dfJaccard$Comparison %in% grupos[2], ]
  
  # Comprueba que hay un único valor por dataset en cada grupo.
  stopifnot(
    !anyNA(g1[[id_col]]), !anyNA(g2[[id_col]]),
    !anyDuplicated(g1[[id_col]]), !anyDuplicated(g2[[id_col]])
  )
  
  # Alinea los valores de ambos grupos por identificador de dataset.
  ids <- intersect(g1[[id_col]], g2[[id_col]])
  x <- g1[["Jaccard index"]][match(ids, g1[[id_col]])]
  y <- g2[["Jaccard index"]][match(ids, g2[[id_col]])]
  completos <- complete.cases(x, y)
  
  data.frame(
    group1 = grupos[1],
    group2 = grupos[2],
    n_pairs = sum(completos),
    p = stats::wilcox.test(x[completos], y[completos], paired = TRUE)$p.value
  )
}))

testsJaccard$p.adj <- stats::p.adjust(testsJaccard$p, method = "BH")
testsJaccard$p.adj.signif <- as.character(stats::symnum(
  testsJaccard$p.adj,
  cutpoints = c(0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 1),
  symbols = c("****", "***", "**", "*", "ns")
))
testsJaccard$y.position <- seq(1.06, 1.28, length.out = nrow(testsJaccard))

testsJaccard


coloresBP <- c("#00204DFF" , "#707173FF", "#F7D03CFF")

pC <- ggplot(dfJaccard, aes(x = Comparison, y = `Jaccard index`, 
                      fill = Comparison, colour = Comparison)) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.35,
    outlier.shape = NA,
    alpha = 0.3, 
    linewidth = 0.4, whisker.linewidth = 0.4, median.linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = coloresBP) + #c("darkgrey","royalblue4", "#A80729"))+
  scale_colour_manual(values = coloresBP) +#c("darkgrey","royalblue4",  "#A80729"))+
  ggrastr::rasterize(
    geom_jitter(
      width = 0.10,
      size = 1.8,
      alpha = 0.65
    ), dpi = 400) +
  # ggpubr::stat_compare_means(
  #   comparisons = comparisonsList,
  #   method = "wilcox.test",
  #   paired = TRUE,
  #   label = "p.signif"
  # ) +
  ggpubr::stat_pvalue_manual(
    testsJaccard,
    label = "p.adj.signif",
    tip.length = 0.01,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1.4),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.25)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jaccard index",
    title = "Global assessment"
  ) +
  ggpubr::theme_pubr(base_size = 16) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",

    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "italic"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5)
```

### {- .toc-ignore}

#### Association with dataset characteristics

To assess whether agreement between rankings varied with dataset characteristics, we fitted a separate linear mixed-effects model for each covariate. Each model included fixed effects for the comparison and the covariate, their interaction, and a random intercept for the dataset:


$$
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 C_j + \beta_2 X_i
       + \beta_3 (C_j \times X_i) + u_i + \varepsilon_{ij}.
$$

In this model,

- $Y_{ij}$ is the Jaccard index for dataset $i$ in comparison $j$.
- $C_j$ denotes the comparison, and $X_i$ denotes the covariate value or level for dataset $i$.
- $\beta_0$ is the intercept.
- $\beta_1$ represents the fixed effect of the comparison.
- $\beta_2$ represents the fixed effect of the covariate.
- $\beta_3$ represents the interaction between the comparison and the covariate.
- $u_i$ is the dataset-specific random intercept, with $u_i \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2)$.
- $\varepsilon_{ij}$ is the residual error, with $\varepsilon_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$.

```{r include=F}
## Data index 
dfIndex <- readxl::read_xlsx( 
  path = "C:/Users/julia/Documents/GitHub/proteomicsNormalizationStudy/Data/_Index.xlsx", 
  sheet = "In", 
  col_names = T)

# Aggregating Specie and Software (necessary for next analysis)
dfIndex <- dfIndex %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    SpecieGrouped = 
      if_else(
        !(Specie %in% c("Mus musculus", "Homo sapiens")), 
        "Others", 
        Specie),
    Software = 
      if_else(
        !(`Analysis Software` %in% c("DIANN", "MaxQuant")),
        "Others", 
        `Analysis Software`),
  )

dfBasales <- dfIndex %>%
    dplyr::select(ID, Acquisition, `MS instrument (summary)`, 
           Software, SpecieGrouped, #`Sample size`, `N groups`,
            `Cell culture`) %>%
  dplyr::rename(Datasets = ID, 
               Instrument = `MS instrument (summary)`,
               CellCulture = `Cell culture`, 
               Specie = SpecieGrouped)

## Merge data
dfComp <- merge(dfJaccard, dfBasales, by = "Datasets")

dfComp <- dfComp %>%
  dplyr::rename(Jaccard = `Jaccard index`)


## Complet model
modeloCompleto <- lme4::lmer(
  Jaccard ~ Comparison *
    (
      Acquisition +
      Instrument +
      CellCulture +
      Software +
      Specie
    ) +
    (1 | Datasets),
  data = dfComp
)

car::Anova(modeloCompleto, type = 3)
```

```{r include=F}
# Individual models
library(car)
dfComp <- dfComp |> dplyr::rename(Species = Specie)
covariables <- c("Acquisition", "Instrument", "CellCulture", "Software", 
                 "Species")
dfComp <- dfComp %>%
  mutate(
    Comparison = factor(Comparison),
    Datasets = factor(Datasets),
    across(all_of(covariables), factor)
  )
resultadosGlobales <- purrr::map_dfr(
  covariables,
  function(covariable) {

    formulaModelo <- as.formula(
      paste0(
        "Jaccard ~ Comparison * ",
        covariable,
        " + (1 | Datasets)"
      )
    )

    modelo <- lme4::lmer(
      formulaModelo,
      data = dfComp
    )

    tabla <- as.data.frame(
      car::Anova(modelo, type = 3)
    )

    terminoInteraccion <- paste0("Comparison:", covariable)

    tibble(
      covariable = covariable,
      pValue = tabla[terminoInteraccion, "Pr(>Chisq)"]
    )
  }
) %>%
  mutate(
    pAdjusted = p.adjust(pValue, method = "BH")
  )
```

The table below reports the unadjusted and adjusted p-values for the coefficients of the comparison-by-covariate interaction for each covariate.

```{r}
js <- c("function(row, data, num, index){", "  var $row = $(row);",

"     }, function(){", "      $(this).css('background-color', 'white');", 
"     }", "    );", "  }else{", "    $row.css('background-color', '#EDFDFA');",

"     }, function(){", "      $(this).css('background-color', '#EDFDFA');", 
"     }", "    );", "  }", "}")
df <- resultadosGlobales
DT::datatable(df, extensions = "Buttons", rownames = F, escape = F,
            options = list(ordering = T, dom = "Brt", scrollY = F,
                            scrollX = F, pageLength = nrow(df),
                            columnDefs = list(list(className = 'dt-center', targets = '_all')),

                            buttons = list(list(extend = "copy", text = "Copiar"),

                            language = list(url = "https://cdn.datatables.net/plug-ins/1.11.5/i18n/es-ES.json"))) |> 
DT::formatStyle(1, font = 'bold') %>% 
  DT::formatRound(2:3, digits = 3)

```

```{r include=F}
library(lme4)
library(emmeans)
library(ggplot2)
library(purrr)

etiquetaP <- ifelse(
      resultadosGlobales$pAdjusted < 0.05,
      " x Comparison: p < 0.05",
      paste0(
        " x Comparison: p = ",
        formatC(
          resultadosGlobales$pAdjusted,
          format = "f",
          digits = 3
        )
      )
    )
etiquetaP <- paste0(resultadosGlobales$covariable, etiquetaP)
names(etiquetaP) <- resultadosGlobales$covariable

allOut <- map(
  covariables,
  function(covariable) {

    formulaModelo <- as.formula(
      paste0(
        "Jaccard ~ Comparison * `",
        covariable,
        "` + (1 | Datasets)"
      )
    )

    modelo <- lmer(
      formulaModelo,
      data = dfComp,
    )

    dfMedias <- emmeans(
      modelo,
      specs = as.formula(
        paste0("~ Comparison * `", covariable, "`")
      )
    ) |>
      as.data.frame()

    p <- ggplot(
      dfMedias,
      aes(
        x = Comparison,
        y = emmean,
        color = .data[[covariable]],
        shape = .data[[covariable]],
        group = .data[[covariable]]
      )
    ) +
      geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
      geom_point(size = 3) +
      geom_errorbar(
        aes(
          ymin = lower.CL,
          ymax = upper.CL
        ),
        width = 0.1
      ) +
      scale_color_manual(values = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(
        n = length(unique(dfComp[,covariable])), 
        name = "Set1")) +
      # scale_color_manual(values = colores[1:length(unique(dfComp[,covariable]))]) +
      labs(
        title = covariable,
        subtitle = etiquetaP[covariable],
        x = NULL,
        y = "Jaccard index",
        color = covariable
      ) +
      theme_minimal(base_size = 14) + 
      ggplot2::theme(
        axis.line = ggplot2::element_line(linewidth = 0.5, colour = "black"), 
        axis.ticks = ggplot2::element_line(linewidth = 0.5, colour = "black"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, vjust = 1, hjust = 1),
        legend.position = "right"
      )
    
    list(
      grafico = p,
      medias = dfMedias, 
      modelo = modelo
    )
  }
)



names(allOut) <- covariables
graficosCovariables <- sapply(allOut, "[[", 1, simplify = F)

allOut[["Etiquetas"]] <- etiquetaP
```
